newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Sentiment seachange sweeps Aussie dlr higher.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Sentiment seachange sweeps Aussie dlr higher.

text.p: The Australian dollar rallied to 5-week highs Friday, a fitting conclusion to a week in which a seachange in sentiment over interest rates looked to have put paid to more than two months of downtrend.

A combination of U.S., Swiss and local bids forced the break of the US$0.7725 barrier but the fundamental impetus sprang from the Reserve Bank's confidence on the economy, backed up by a string of robust data, which minified the risk of a rate cut.
Dealers felt the rally confirmed the currency had found bottom at US$0.7550 and, although few thought it was going to romp higher, they did see scope to reach 78 cents soon.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar had leapt to US$0.7740/45, its highest local close since January 20, from an early US$0.7725/30 and US$0.7685/90 late here Thursday.
Support was now expected around US$0.7675, which provided stiff resistance on the way up, while the currency would have to breach US$0.7630 to reverse the improving trend.

On the crosses the local currency actually bucked a bout of profit-taking on the U.S. dollar, suggesting to dealers it was attracting demand of its own. The view was backed up by signs of an ongoing switch by offshore funds into the A$ and out of its fellow dollar-bloc member from Canada.
The dollar finished firm at 95.16/26 yen from 95.11/21 late Thursday after recovering from an early low around 94.61 low, and that was despite a one yen drop in the US$.

It also pushed to 1.1434/46 Swiss francs from 1.1341/57, its first venture above 1.1400 since May 1992, and to 59.3 in trade weighted terms from 59.0 late Thursday and a 58.0 low earlier this month. The switch by offshore funds out of the Canadian dollar propelled it to C$1.0545/56 from C$1.0449/60, its best level in five weeks.
Much of this movement reflected a seachange in sentiment on the future of the Australian economy and monetary polcy.
Just a month ago the market was betting the RBA would have to cut rates again to revive a deteriorating economic position.

But a run of surprisingly upbeat data and an bullish outlook from the RBA this week had quashed all thought of another easing and seen money rates and bond yields rise sharply, so widening the interest differential enjoyed by the currency.

The trend was amplified by subdued U.S. inflation data which greatly lessened the risk of a Fed hike, and continued economic weakness in much of Europe which promised to keep rates there low. One result was the spread on the two-year bonds yawned to 70 basis points from less than 40 a few weeks ago.

This was potentially an important development since this was the part of the curve favoured by Japanese investors and 40 basis points was believed to be the threshold beneath which they rated A$ issues as too risky.
The narrowing in the gap was partly why the flow of yen/A$ samurai issues had dried up this year, so the widening, if sustained, might even tempt back Japanese investors.

They noted Nomura had launched a reverse dual currency samurai bond overnight which paid interest in A$ and although small at just 5.0 billion yen, it was the first to feature the A$ since the start of January.

Even the suggestion of returning demand could prove self fulfilling since it would tend to push the dollar higher and add the promise of currency gains to the relatively high yield such samurais already offered.
The next major domestic economic data of note was capital expenditure data for Q4 on Thursday which should confirm the very strong outlook for business investment in 1997.
Also out next week was the Department of Inustrial Relations report on wage trends in enterprise bargaining, an important guide to wage pressures in the private sector.
